summary: This informational memo analyses the security threats relevant to the NSIS signalling protocols. It aims to help readers understand the security considerations in the NSIS requirements, framework and protocol documents.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4081 analyzes ways attackers could misuse Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS). It examines who communicates with whom, what information can be exposed or changed, and how signaling state could be abused.

what are the security threats to nsis

subtitle: Threat scenarios that NSIS designers need to consider when signaling installs network state.

tldr.problem: NSIS signaling can install or change state at nodes along a data path, so attackers may try to disrupt service, use resources without authorization, or learn network information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes communication and trust relationships, then analyzes four generic signaling threats and eleven NSIS-specific threat scenarios.
tldr.outcome: This is a threat analysis, not a protocol specification or a report of vulnerabilities in specific NSIS components. It is intended to inform protocol design alongside the requirements and framework documents.

today: RFC 4081 is an Informational RFC published in June 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it is a threat analysis, not an NSIS protocol specification.

sections.title: Purpose and Limits of the Analysis
sections.content:
The RFC identifies security threats that NSIS protocol designers need to consider. NSIS signaling can install or manipulate state at nodes along a network path.

The document does not assess every possible signaling application and does not describe vulnerabilities in specific parts of the NSIS protocol suite. The QoS and NAT/Firewall signaling-layer protocols need their own trust models and threat assessments.
sections.plainLanguage: This document lists threats that designers of NSIS protocols should consider. It is a general analysis, not a report about a specific implementation or vulnerability.

sections.title: Communication Paths and Trust
sections.content:
NSIS signaling may pass between an Initiator and a Responder through intermediate NSIS nodes. The security needed depends on the relationship between those parties and on whether communication stays within one administrative domain or crosses domains.

The RFC distinguishes first-peer, intra-domain, inter-domain, end-to-middle, middle-to-middle, and end-to-end relationships. Intermediate nodes need to process signaling, so protecting an entire message end-to-end may not be feasible: those nodes may need to inspect or change parts of it.
sections.plainLanguage: A signaling message can pass through several network operators and intermediate nodes. Some nodes need to inspect or change it, so security depends on which parts of the path and message must be protected.

sections.title: Generic Threats to Signaling
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four generic threats: man-in-the-middle attacks, replay of signaling messages, injection or modification of messages, and insecure negotiation of security parameters.

An attacker could impersonate a peer while a security association is established, replay an old request, delay or alter a message, or change a negotiation so that weaker protection is selected. Replaying messages after a node loses state can also create problems even when replay protection is used.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker may impersonate a participant, replay an old message, alter a message, or interfere with security negotiation. The RFC explains these as risks that signaling designs must address.

sections.title: Resource Exhaustion and Information Exposure
sections.content:
The NSIS-specific scenarios include flooding. An attacker can make nodes process bogus messages, allocate state, or perform costly work before rejecting a request. Messages may also trigger requests to policy, directory, or authentication servers.

Eavesdropping can reveal information such as communication patterns, user identities, policy rules, or network configuration. Signaling can also expose network topology, and using discovery messages can direct traffic toward a node that is not the next NSIS-aware node on the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Fake requests can consume memory, processing time, or network resources. Listening to signaling can also reveal information about users, policies, and network structure.

sections.title: Identity, Authorization, and Session Ownership
sections.content:
Identity spoofing can cause resources to be charged to another user, alter the flow identifier used for a reservation, or let forged data use state installed for a legitimate flow. Unprotected authorization information can also be stolen or changed.

If an attacker learns a session identifier, a node may not be able to tell whether a later request comes from the session's owner. The RFC also discusses missing non-repudiation, malicious NSIS nodes, denial of service, and attacks on the transport layer protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A forged identity or stolen session identifier can let an attacker misuse or change a reservation. Authorization information needs protection, and a compromised network node can create risks beyond its own messages.

sections.title: Security Capabilities for NSIS Designs
sections.content:
The RFC says designers should consider authentication, key establishment, message integrity, replay protection, confidentiality, authorization, and denial-of-service precautions. The importance of each threat depends on the application and deployment environment.

The related NSIS security requirements are in RFC 3726. Each signaling application still needs to describe the trust relationships and threats specific to its use.
sections.plainLanguage: Different NSIS uses need different protections. Designers should select security capabilities for their environment and document the threats specific to each application.
